title: Sarcopenia and knee osteoarthritis: the frailty overlap (UK)
meta_title: Sarcopenia and knee osteoarthritis: the frailty overlap (UK)
meta_description: How age-related muscle loss (sarcopenia) and knee osteoarthritis affect each other, and how strength exercise and good nutrition can help in later life.
excerpt: How age-related muscle loss (sarcopenia) and knee osteoarthritis affect each other, and how strength exercise and good nutrition can help in later life.
direct_answer: Sarcopenia is the loss of muscle strength and mass with age. Weak thigh muscles put more strain on the knee, and knee pain can lead to less activity and more muscle loss. Regular strengthening exercise, staying active and eating enough protein can help break this cycle.
author: Louis Maxwell

content:
Knee osteoarthritis is common in later life, and so is gradual muscle loss. When they happen together, standing up, climbing stairs and walking can get harder.

This guide explains how the two conditions overlap and what helps. It is educational information, not a diagnosis or personal treatment plan.

How they affect each other

  • Strong thigh muscles help support and protect the knee.
  • Pain can lead to moving less.
  • Moving less leads to further muscle loss.
  • Weak muscles make falls and loss of independence more likely.

Signs to notice

  • Difficulty getting up from a chair without using your arms.
  • Slower walking.
  • Difficulty with stairs or carrying shopping.
  • Unplanned weight loss or reduced appetite.

What helps

  • NICE recommends exercise, including muscle strengthening, as a core treatment for osteoarthritis.
  • Simple exercises such as sit-to-stand and leg raises, done regularly, can build strength.
  • Start gently and build up gradually. Some discomfort is normal, but pain should settle afterwards.
  • Eat regular meals that include protein, such as fish, eggs, beans, dairy or meat.
  • Ask about physiotherapy or a strength and balance class.

Getting help

Talk to your GP if you are losing weight, getting weaker or falling. They can check for other causes and refer you for physiotherapy, dietetic advice or a frailty review.

When to get help

  • Call 999 for chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of a stroke, or a fall with a possible serious injury.
  • Get urgent advice the same day (NHS 111 or your GP) for sudden confusion, a sudden drop in mobility, or a hot, swollen joint with fever.
  • See your GP for a steady decline over weeks, unplanned weight loss or repeated falls.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Is it too late to build muscle?

Muscle strength can improve at any age with regular exercise.

Will exercise damage my knee?

Exercise is recommended for knee osteoarthritis and does not usually cause harm.

Sources and further reading

  • NICE NG226: Osteoarthritis in over 16s
